proof:
# Exact shape facts and limits for the optimized median capacity

Let V(y) be the maximum halfspace depth at y among all median-pair targets
from a fixed finite uniform convex-fiber family.

## 1. Raw concavity and powers above 1/d fail

Take C=[0,1] times K, with K a d-dimensional simplex, d>=2, and select
the median fiber z0=0. Its probability half-marginals are entirely in
fiber 0 and fiber 1, respectively. For EVERY pair, T(p,q)=p. Thus the
target is fixed to uniform K regardless of the coupling. This is a
two-fiber example; a single original fiber would allow self-couplings and
would not give a fixed uniform target.

Let a be a vertex and g the simplex centroid. Then V(a)=0 and
V(g)=gamma_d. The hyperplane through y_t=(1-t)a+t g parallel to the
opposite facet cuts off a homothetic vertex simplex of volume fraction
t^d gamma_d. Therefore

    V(y_t)<=t^d gamma_d,       0<t<1.

For any p>1/d this yields

    V(y_t)^p < t gamma_d^p
               =(1-t)V(a)^p+t V(g)^p.

Consequently no universal concavity of V^p is possible for p>1/d; in
particular raw concavity fails in every d>=2. All bounds here are exact.
Ordinary Brunn-Minkowski shows that V^(1/d) is concave for a FIXED uniform
convex target: for each fixed normal the relevant cap volumes have that
concavity, and the infimum of concave functions is concave. This does not
establish the same property for optimized targets with several pair strata.

## 2. One-dimensional low superlevels are always intervals

For ANY convex family F of probability measures on the line, define

    U(y)=sup_(nu in F) min(nu((-infinity,y]),nu([y,infinity))).

For every 0<=t<=1/2 the set {y:U(y)>=t} is an interval if the suprema
are attained. Without attainment, the strict superlevel {U>t} is an
interval for t<1/2, and the same proof applies to attained membership.

Here is the direct argument in the attained case. Suppose y_1<y<y_2
and nu_1,nu_2 have depths at least t at y_1,y_2. Then the left mass of
nu_1 at y is at least t and the right mass of nu_2 at y is at least t.
If either measure already has both masses at least t, nothing remains.
Otherwise the right mass of nu_1 is below t and the left mass of nu_2
is below t. The left mass varies affinely along their mixtures, so choose
a mixture whose left mass is exactly t. Its right mass is at least
1-t>=t, since the two closed rays cover the line. This mixture belongs
to F and proves U(y)>=t. Atoms and their double counting only improve
the inequality.

The median-pair target family is convex and weakly compact, and its
fixed-center optima are attained. Hence V has convex superlevels at
every t<=1/2 when d=1, regardless of the number of integer pair strata.
The same holds for the trimmed target family. In particular this covers
the relevant target level gamma_1=1/2.

For an arbitrary convex law family, levels above 1/2 need not be convex:
take all mixtures of delta_0 and delta_1. Its optimized depth is one at
the two endpoints and one half at every point strictly between them.
This last example is not claimed to be realizable by the required
uniform source fibers. It marks only the limit of the general convex-law
argument.

## 3. Numerical caution

The exploratory script `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/transport_capacity_interval_screen.py` replaces
uniform interval sources by point grids. Its apparent sharp spikes depend
on exact coincidences of grid-pair means with the tested center, so they
do not certify shape failures for the continuous-source problem. No
numerical output of that script is used in either result above. Whether
the 1/d power or all relevant superlevels retain a stronger shape property
for higher-dimensional optimized median targets is not settled here.

## 4. Every positive-power concavity fails for the optimized TRIMMED family

This stronger obstruction concerns the trimmed value, not the unrestricted
median coupling value. Let all three fibers A=B=C be the standard triangle
K={(x_1,x_2):x_1,x_2>=0,x_1+x_2<=1}. Divide every volume by |K|, so its
uniform measure kappa has mass one. The trimmed target has the form

    nu=(kappa+T#pi)/(3/2),

where pi has mass 1/2 and both marginals are dominated by kappa.

Put y_t=(t,t), 1/4<=t<=1/3. Its barycentric coordinates are
(1-2t,t,t). The reflection overlap D_t=K intersect (2y_t-K) has normalized
area

    kappa(D_t)=1-(4t-1)^2-2(1-2t)^2
               =-2+16t-24t^2 >=1/2.                    (1)

Indeed D_t is given by barycentric upper bounds x_i<=2lambda_i. On this
t interval the three excluded corner triangles have the displayed squared
area fractions and disjoint interiors; sums of any two lambda_i are at
least one half. Formula (1) is also obtained directly by their subtraction.

Choose the submeasure eta=[(1/2)/kappa(D_t)]1_(D_t) kappa. Reflection
about y_t preserves eta, so pi=(id,x->2y_t-x)#eta is admissible and
T#pi=(1/2)delta_(y_t). This explicitly realizes the maximal residual atom.

The ordinary normalized triangle depth at y_t is exactly 4t^2. Here is
a cap certificate for both directions of that assertion. A vertex-i cap
with intercept fractions r,s on its adjacent edges contains y only if
lambda_j/r+lambda_k/s<=1. It therefore has area fraction rs>=4lambda_j
lambda_k, by the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality. Equality is obtained
at r=2lambda_j,s=2lambda_k; these are at most one in this interval. The
smallest such fraction is 4t^2, attained by x_1+x_2<=2t.

A cap containing two vertices is the complement of an open vertex cap.
For excluded vertex i, maximizing the complementary product rs subject to
lambda_j/r+lambda_k/s>=1 and r,s<=1 occurs at r=1 or s=1. To check this,
on the equality curve the product is lambda_k r^2/(r-lambda_j), a convex
function of r, so its maximum on the permitted interval is at an endpoint.
The two-vertex cap fraction is consequently at least
lambda_i/[1-min(lambda_j,lambda_k)]. In the present family this is at
least t/(1-t)>=4t^2, since 4t(1-t)<=1. All cap orientations are covered;
a cap may always be shrunk until its boundary passes through y.

For ANY admissible residual measure of mass one half, a smallest base cap
gives depth at y_t at most (4t^2+1/2)/(3/2). The explicit atom coupling
attains this bound, because every closed cap containing y_t includes its
entire residual atom. Thus the exact optimized trimmed value is

    V_trim(y_t)=(4t^2+1/2)/(3/2),       1/4<=t<=1/3.      (2)

For every p>0, the second derivative of (4t^2+1/2)^p is

    8p(4t^2+1/2)^(p-2)[1/2+4(2p-1)t^2]>0

on the entire interval: its bracket is at least 1/2-4/9>0. Hence
V_trim^p is strictly convex there and cannot be concave for ANY positive
power p. This includes p=1/d=1/2. The construction uses actual compatible
uniform fibers and exact coupling and cap upper certificates.

The unrestricted family also permits central-central pairs and can have
a larger optimized value. No equality between its value and (2) has been
proved, so this section does not refute unrestricted positive-power
concavity or quasiconcavity.
